basics.name: Maker adhesive guides and tests for 3D prints and hobby materials: Prusa's 'The Great Guide to Gluing and Assembling 3D Prints' (with tensile tests) and the Prusa Knowledge Base material pages; CNC Kitchen's glue and solvent-bonding tests; and woodworking glue guides (Woodcraft glue chart, Rockler 'Understanding Wood Glue'), plus smaller hobby tests (MakerBuildIt) and the thistothat.com glue picker
basics.url: Main page: https://blog.prusa3d.com/the-great-guide-to-gluing-and-assembling-3d-prints_44908/ (opened). Also opened: Prusa KB https://help.prusa3d.com/article/pla_2062 , https://help.prusa3d.com/article/petg_2059 and https://help.prusa3d.com/article/asa_1809 ; CNC Kitchen https://www.cnckitchen.com/blog/can-acetone-glue-layers-of-3d-prints-together ; Hackaday write-up of CNC Kitchen's glue video https://hackaday.com/2019/12/28/stronger-3d-prints-glue-or-carbon-fiber/ (video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wN1AFG08P28 , title confirmed via YouTube oEmbed); Woodcraft https://www.woodcraft.com/blogs/sanding-finishing/complete-guide-to-woodworking-glues ; Rockler https://www.rockler.com/learn/understanding-wood-glue ; MakerBuildIt https://makerbuildit.com/blogs/3d-printing/strongest-glue-for-3d-printed-parts ; Formlabs https://formlabs.com/blog/advanced-3dp-techniques/ ; This to That https://www.thistothat.com/
basics.resource_type: Mixed maker guides: manufacturer blog and knowledge base (Prusa, Formlabs), video channel with a test blog (CNC Kitchen), retailer guides (Woodcraft, Rockler), a hobby test blog (MakerBuildIt) and a small interactive tool (This to That)
basics.cost: Free (no login needed for any page opened)

basics.year: Prusa gluing guide by Vladimír Kafka, published 5 February 2021, modified 23 April 2021. Prusa KB material pages are live in 2026 (edit dates not shown). CNC Kitchen glue-and-carbon-fibre video about December 2019 (Hackaday write-up 28 December 2019); acetone layer-bonding blog post dated 20 August 2022. Woodcraft and Rockler guides are undated, with 2026 page footers [uncertain]. thistothat.com has been running since 1999
basics.image_license: All rights reserved (the authors' own photos of glued samples, test rigs and glue products; CNC Kitchen videos on YouTube under the standard YouTube licence). No openly licensed images found
basics.authority_level: Manufacturer (Prusa Research, Formlabs) and educator/tester (CNC Kitchen, an engineer who runs repeatable strength tests on a DIY universal test machine). Woodworking retailers (Woodcraft, Rockler) are community or trade level; MakerBuildIt and thistothat.com are community or unvetted. For peer-reviewed data on bonded prints, see Polymers 2025, 17(6), 768 (doi:10.3390/polym17060768), a CC BY single-lap-joint study of epoxy-bonded 3D-printed ABS and PLA (abstract read via Europe PMC)

coverage.covers: Hobby adhesive TYPES for 3D-printed plastics, resin and wood, with test results. PRUSA GUIDE: 3 main types in depth (cyanoacrylate/CA, including gel, rubber-filled, odourless/foam-safe and extra-thin capillary grades, plus debonders; solvent glues, both extra-thin and thick modeller's cements, and capillary gluing; two-part epoxy). It briefly lists PVA wood glue, contact cement, hot glue, silicone, 'resin + UV light', and construction ('mounting') adhesive for very large prints. It also covers non-permanent options (screws, magnets, pausing the print to embed nuts or magnets), and ends with a tensile test of 12 glues on PLA, PETG and ASA. PRUSA KB material pages: which solvent glues or welds which filament (ASA and ABS with acetone; some PLA partly with acetone, or superglue; PETG dissolves only in lab chemicals such as dichloromethane). CNC KITCHEN: glue and carbon-fibre reinforcement of printed hooks (thin and thick CA, epoxy), and acetone/IPA solvent bonding of ABS and PVB. WOODWORKING: Woodcraft's chart compares 10 wood glues (simple PVA, three compound PVAs (Titebond Original, II and III style), dry/hot hide glue, liquid hide glue, polyurethane, epoxy, urea-formaldehyde, CA) on pot life, open time, clamp/cure time, colour, cleanup, water resistance, shelf life and cost, plus advice on creep, toxicity, speed, temperature, water and gap filling. Rockler describes 6 types (PVA, aliphatic resin, epoxy, polyurethane, CA, hide glue). EXTRAS: MakerBuildIt snap and twist tests on PLA (hot glue, CA, '3D Gloop', a plastics epoxy, polyurethane glue, construction adhesive); Formlabs' 'resin plus 405 nm laser' as a glue for resin prints; thistothat.com's 11-by-11 material-pair glue picker
coverage.organisation: Prusa guide: by glue type (CA → solvent → epoxy → others → non-permanent → test table), each with how it works, which product to choose, and warnings and tips, plus a table of contents. Prusa KB: one page per filament, with gluing and smoothing notes inside. CNC Kitchen: one experiment per video or blog post, with a TL;DR summary, method, results and chart. Woodcraft: a side-by-side comparison chart, then 'Avoid / Try' advice by situation (creep, health, speed, cold, water, gaps), which works well for beginners. thistothat.com: pick 'this' material and 'that' material from two drop-downs. All are easy for beginners because they start from the material or job, not the chemistry
coverage.scope_match: high: exactly the project's adhesive scope (types compared by material and use, especially PLA, PETG, ABS/ASA, resin and wood), with real test numbers. The only drawbacks are product and brand focus (the Prusa test names products, not just types), and that the sources are scattered
coverage.taxonomy_used: Informal, by how the glue works. Prusa: 3 main groups (cyanoacrylate, solvent-based, two-part epoxy) plus an 'other' list (PVA, contact cement, hot glue, silicone, UV resin, construction adhesive) and non-permanent assembly. Woodcraft: 10 columns grouped by chemistry (PVA simple and compound, hide dry and liquid, polyurethane, epoxy, urea-formaldehyde, CA). Rockler: 6 types. thistothat.com: by material pair (11 material classes: ceramic, fabric, glass, leather, metal, paper, plastic, rubber, styrofoam, vinyl, wood)
coverage.example_types: cyanoacrylate / superglue (thin, medium, gel, rubber-toughened, odourless/foam-safe, extra-thin capillary); CA debonder (solvent that undoes CA); solvent welding / solvent cement (acetone for ABS and ASA, also some PLA; limonene for HIPS; isopropyl alcohol for PVB; polystyrene modeller's cement); 'ABS juice' (plastic dissolved in solvent as a thick glue); capillary gluing with extra-thin cement or CA; two-part epoxy (5-minute and slow-cure, as a coating or filler); CA tack points plus epoxy fill (hybrid); PVA white glue; aliphatic resin (yellow) wood glue, water-resistant Type II and waterproof Type I; hot hide glue and liquid hide glue (reversible); polyurethane foaming glue (moisture-cure); urea-formaldehyde (resin) glue for veneer and bent laminations; contact cement (suggested for flexible TPU); hot-melt glue; silicone adhesive; construction (mounting) adhesive for large prints; UV-cured resin as glue for resin prints (405 nm laser); methacrylate 'plastic welder' (reader suggestion for PETG and ABS, not tested)
coverage.making_methods: 3D printing (FDM/FFF, with some SLA/resin) is the main focus; also woodworking; scale modelling and RC hobby practice feeds into the Prusa guide
coverage.item_count: Prusa guide: 3 main types, 6 'other' types, 12 products tensile-tested on 3 materials. Prusa KB: 1 page per filament (dozens of materials). CNC Kitchen: 2 relevant glue/solvent test pieces found (the site has about 125 blog posts in total). Woodcraft: 10 glue columns by 9 property rows. Rockler: 6 types. MakerBuildIt: 7 glues on PLA. thistothat.com: 11 × 11 material pairs (about 66 unique combinations)
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: Adhesive types by material, the main subject. PLA: CA was best in Prusa's test (about 9.5 to 10.2 MPa for the three best CAs (other CAs 5.1 to 8.0), versus 5.0 to 6.3 MPa for 5-minute epoxies and 0.9 to 4.9 MPa for solvent or 'all plastics' glues). Some PLA can be glued with acetone (Prusa guide and KB). MakerBuildIt: CA, 3D Gloop and a plastics epoxy all broke the PLA before the bond failed; hot glue, a construction adhesive and 'clear Gorilla Glue' (chemistry not stated) failed, and foaming polyurethane glue held when twisted but snapped cleanly and pushed parts out of line; hot glue can deform PLA. CNC Kitchen: thin CA reached 58 kg on a PLA-blend hook versus about 53 kg untreated; epoxy cracked first, so no gain. PETG: CA was clearly best (13.1 and 12.6 MPa for the top two), and there's no hobby solvent (the Prusa guide says PETG is 'inert to all chemicals normally available to a hobbyist'; the KB says it dissolves only in dichloromethane in a lab). ABS/ASA: acetone solvent-welds (Prusa KB). CNC Kitchen found an acetone repair of ABS reached 17 MPa, as strong as the part's own layer bond (19 MPa), and 2 of 3 samples broke beside the joint. But brushing acetone on every layer while printing gave only 6 MPa (about 15% of flat-printed strength). Prusa's ASA test: extra-thin CA 11.3 MPa, standard CA 9.4, polystyrene poly cement 7.4, Tamiya extra-thin 6.1; one modeller's cement didn't bond ASA at all. HIPS: limonene. PVB: isopropyl alcohol. Resin (SLA): CA works (gel CA is recommended because the bond is almost instant), or liquid resin cured with a 405 nm laser (Formlabs). TPU: CA works if the mating faces are fairly stiff, and contact cement is suggested. Styrofoam: ordinary CA melts it, so use odourless/foam-safe CA. Wood: PVA for indoor joinery, Type II/III for damp, epoxy for gaps and constant water, polyurethane for wet wood or wood to non-wood, hide glue for reversible repairs, urea-formaldehyde for creep-free laminations, CA for quick fixes but brittle. Heat: ordinary CA keeps about 50% of its strength at 80 °C and about 20% at 100 °C; heat-resistant CA keeps 80% at 120 °C; CA goes brittle when frozen. Hand-release / reversible: CA debonders or acetone (test first); freezing snaps CA joints; hide glue with heat and water; screws and magnets as the non-permanent option. Not covered: torque-limiting, ratchet, detent, over-centre, gears, powered connectors
coverage.entry_structure: Prusa guide sections: how the glue type works → pros and cons (set time, strength in tension versus shear or peel, sanding, blooming or frosting, shelf life, storage) → product examples with one-line verdicts → warnings, tips and fun facts. Then a results table (MPa per glue for PLA, PETG and ASA). CNC Kitchen: TL;DR, method, reference samples, results chart, discussion of failure, and a video. Woodcraft: chart rows (pot life, open time, clamp/cure time, colour, cleanup, water resistance, shelf life, cost, notes) plus Avoid/Try blocks
coverage.audience_level: hobbyist (FDM and resin printer owners, scale modellers, cosplay, DIY woodworkers)

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: high: plain language, product photos, clear 'do this, not that' advice, and practical tips (breathe on CA to speed it up, clean off and restart if the fit is wrong after a few seconds, keep CA fumes away to avoid white frosting). Some brand names are local to the Czech Republic, and the numbers need context (single samples)
usefulness.has_images: yes: good-quality photos of products, glued joints, CA frosting and test samples (Prusa); test rigs, fracture surfaces and result charts (CNC Kitchen); the Woodcraft chart. No diagrams of joint geometry
usefulness.has_animations: Video: CNC Kitchen YouTube tests ('STRONGER 3D Prints with GLUE? (and CARBON FIBERS)', and the acetone layer-bonding video); the Prusa guide embeds a video of large multi-part prints; MakerBuildIt is a video-based test. No interactive models
usefulness.gaps: No single place with all types × all materials. Prusa's test has one quick sample per cell and names products, not grades. No shear or peel data, only tension (and the guide itself notes CA is weak in shear, peel and torsion). Thin coverage of PETG alternatives (methacrylate structural adhesives are only a reader comment), of nylon, polycarbonate and TPU, and of bonding prints to metal, wood or fabric. Almost no joint design advice (overlap area, keys, pins, dovetails to help the glue). CNC Kitchen has no dedicated multi-glue comparison blog post (the glue data is from one 2019 video summarised by Hackaday). Woodworking guides don't mention printed plastics. thistothat.com gives brand names, and lumps all plastics into one class
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: Yes. Stable URLs: the Prusa guide (one URL, with section headings but no anchors seen [uncertain]); Prusa KB per-material pages such as https://help.prusa3d.com/article/asa_1809 (ASA: glue/weld with acetone); CNC Kitchen per-test posts; the Woodcraft chart page. Good to link from CA, solvent-welding, epoxy, PVA and hide-glue entries
usefulness.reusable_data: Scrape-only. The Prusa tensile table (12 glues × 3 materials, MPa) and the Woodcraft chart (10 glues × 9 properties) are small enough to cite as facts with attribution, but not to copy wholesale (all rights reserved). No API or dataset. thistothat.com results come from a simple query URL (cgi-bin/glue.cgi?this=Plastic&that=Wood), but the content is copyrighted
usefulness.maintained: All online in September 2026. The Prusa guide hasn't been updated since April 2021 (it promised more alternatives later; a reader's methacrylate suggestion was acknowledged). The Prusa KB is maintained. CNC Kitchen is active (sitemap updated September 2026). Woodcraft and Rockler pages are live. thistothat.com shows a 1999–2024 copyright
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) A material-by-glue matrix with test numbers, like Prusa's MPa table, but by TYPE rather than brand, with the source per cell. (2) Woodcraft's 'Avoid / Try' blocks per situation (long-term load or creep, outdoor/water, gaps, cold shop, health, need for speed): great flow-chart branches. (3) Split the property columns: open time, clamp time, full cure time, gap filling, cleanup, water resistance, reversibility. (4) thistothat.com's 'this material + that material' two-drop-down picker as a model for the adhesive part of the flow chart. (5) Show failure location (glue failed versus the part broke next to the glue) as the real measure of a good joint (CNC Kitchen, MakerBuildIt). (6) 'Can I undo it?' notes (debonder, freezer, heat). (7) Hybrid tips: CA tack points plus epoxy fill; glue plus screws, inserts or magnets. (8) Warn about 'look-alike product names' (e.g. one product line with both CA and solvent versions) to push readers to think in types
usefulness.design_rules_given: Yes, some numbers: Prusa tensile strengths per glue for PLA, PETG and ASA (about 0.9 to 13.1 MPa); CA hardness develops over 8 to 24 hours; CA heat derating (50% at 80 °C, 20% at 100 °C; heat-resistant CA 80% at 120 °C); epoxy cure times from under 90 seconds to over 12 hours. CNC Kitchen: ABS 41 MPa flat versus 19 MPa across layers, acetone-bonded 17 MPa; hook loads (untreated about 53 kg versus thin CA 58 kg). Woodcraft: open time, clamp time and cure time per glue (e.g. PVA 5 to 10 minutes open, 30 to 60 minutes clamp, 24 hours cure; epoxy 4 to 50 minutes pot life); PVAs need above about 50 °F (10 °C), Titebond III-type down to 45 °F, some epoxies down to 35 °F; epoxy and UF stable to about 200 °F and 180 °F; at least 50% of the joint faces should be in contact. Peer-reviewed extra: epoxy single-lap joints on printed PLA reached 2.7 to 3.4 kN and ABS 1.4 to 1.7 kN, strongest when cured at 80 °C for 1 hour (Polymers 2025)
usefulness.file_formats: HTML articles, YouTube video, tables in HTML (no downloadable data)
usefulness.terminology_value: medium: good for the hobby names and their aliases (CA = superglue = instant glue; accelerator/activator ('kicker'); debonder; extra-thin cement; capillary gluing; frosting/blooming; gel CA; foam-safe CA; yellow glue = aliphatic resin; Type I (waterproof) versus Type II (water-resistant); open time, pot life, clamp time, creep; chalk temperature (the temperature below which PVA dries white and fails)). Not an authority for chemistry names, so use the adhesive reference works item for those
usefulness.decision_support: Prusa: a comparison table of test results plus pros-and-cons prose, but no selector. Woodcraft: a side-by-side comparison chart plus situation-based Avoid/Try rules (effectively a decision list). thistothat.com: a two-drop-down material-pair selector that returns recommended glue products, 'faster' alternatives, 'less toxic' alternatives and tips (e.g. plastic to wood: silicone-based glue for strongest, 5-minute epoxy for faster, contact cement as the less toxic option, clamp, and sand smooth plastic with 120 grit)
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: The Prusa guide draws on scale-modelling and RC hobby practice (debonders, capillary cement, Tamiya, Humbrol). Its test uses the same printed samples and machine as Prusa's annealing article. CNC Kitchen's solvent tests follow on from his earlier acetone-smoothing tests. Hackaday summarises the CNC Kitchen glue video, so cite the video as the original. Woodcraft and Rockler overlap with each other and with Titebond maker literature. Overlaps with the adhesive reference works item (ASC, Petrie, Wikipedia) for the family names; Wikipedia's 'Adhesive' article links to thistothat.com. Many third-party 'best glue for PLA' blogs (All3DP, 3DSourced and others) repeat the same CA / epoxy / solvent advice, so they don't need separate counting [uncertain]
